claims.text: Corrosion resistance in steels used for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is governed by the formation and stability of a continuous chromium-rich passive oxide layer.
The chromium-rich passive layer prevents corrosive species from penetrating to the underlying steel.
Relevant commercial steel alloys typically contain 10–25% chromium.
The governing structural mediator is an ultrathin, adherent, Cr2O3-rich surface film.
The Cr2O3-rich film acts as a physical and chemical barrier.
The passive film impedes diffusion of oxygen and aggressive ions to the underlying steel.
Impeded transport through the passive film dramatically reduces the corrosion rate.
Passive-film integrity and chemical stability are critical to maintaining corrosion resistance.
Samples retaining or regenerating the passive film will have lower corrosion rates than samples with disrupted films.
The predicted lower corrosion rate will be observable through reduced weight loss, reduced pit depth, and electrochemical-impedance behavior consistent with stronger barrier properties.
Lower chromium content produces a less robust passive film.
Steels with lower or non-optimized chromium content fail to form an effective passive layer and consequently corrode faster under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism should hold for commercial steels with sufficient chromium under moderate temperatures and non-extreme pH conditions.
Extreme radiation or severe chemical environments may destabilize passive films and place the system outside the hypothesis's domain.
Nickel or molybdenum may modify the proposed passivation mechanism.
Selective removal or thinning of the passive film should cause a statistically detectable increase in corrosion relative to an intact-film control, unless the film successfully regenerates.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome allows a film-removed sample to regain low corrosion by successful passive-film regeneration, but the falsification rule treats the absence of increased corrosion or of a post-exposure film difference as falsifying. Equal outcomes and similar post-exposure films could therefore be either a predicted result of regeneration or a falsifying result.
